hints.hint: Keep the candidate set finite and apply announcements in chronological order, recomputing information sets after each. Critical: if a displayed number is not labelled (e.g. could be the sum or the product), the speakers share that ambiguity, so a candidate is (my own value, which reading holds). "I don't know" then means my own value still admits two or more distinct partners, counting across readings; turn that into an arithmetic test on my own value (divisibility, positivity, range) and keep only values that pass. If every reading seems contradictory, you wrongly assumed the speakers knew the label. Never box a number just because it appeared in your enumeration: check the survivor satisfies every statement first.

Divide by the appropriate power of the variable and introduce the ratio w=(z-1)/z. The equation then restricts w to a fixed finite set on a circle. Solve the Möbius relation for z in terms of w, and characterize the image locus geometrically (or by an equation in x and y). Use all allowed roots and check exceptional values before extracting the requested circle parameter.

Fix coordinates once, pinned point at the origin; never restart the setup. For fixed-area pieces, union = sum minus overlap, so maximize the union by minimizing overlap. Beware the trap of assuming the bigger shape swallows the smaller one: a polygon vertex is only a wedge of its interior angle, so beyond that apex the shape covers nothing. Test one concrete point on the far side before concluding containment. When the apex sits at a center of n-fold rotational symmetry, that 2pi/n wedge cuts off exactly 1/n of the region at every rotation angle, so there is nothing to optimize. Then commit to one exact fraction and stop.

Extremal "how long / how many at most" problems need two halves: an upper bound and a matching construction. State both targets before computing. For bounds, express the required pattern as one closed form in the index (an arithmetic progression is A+B*index), subtract it from each candidate function, and count zeros: a degree-d polynomial minus an affine function is still degree d and not identically zero, so it can match at most d indices. When several functions are available, each contributes its own cap, so add the caps over all functions - do not stop at one function's cap, and do not use the function count alone. Do not chase consecutive differences; that only limits reuse of a single function. Then realize the bound by cutting the index range into consecutive blocks and interpolating one function per block. Commit to this route early instead of enumerating cases.

First substitute the two known graph points to determine the parameters of the logarithmic fractional-linear function. Derive the parallelogram translation from oriented vectors, impose both graph equations, and eliminate one coordinate using the logarithm. Solve the remaining scalar relation while respecting the domain, then compute the area from a determinant. Verify that the resulting points lie on the correct branches.

Trap: asserting symmetry. "Each item is equally likely in any position", or "n! orderings so 1/n!", is a guess. A process random over MOVES is rarely uniform over OUTCOMES.

Instead: (1) Pin mechanics first — what move is legal, which item it touches (top of stack only?), and whether the target position means the FIRST or LAST arrival. Derive that from the stacking rule; never guess. (2) Turn the event into an exact constraint on the move sequence, e.g. "moves strictly alternate" or "exactly k source-moves precede the first sink-move". (3) Count only genuinely free 50/50 choices; forced moves (source or sink empty) contribute factor 1, giving 1/2^(free choices), not 1/n or 1/n!. (4) Check n=2 by full enumeration. Re-derive each part from scratch — same setup, different constraint.

Compute before theorizing. Replace the large size by n = 2, then 3; write that tiny system out and solve it exactly. Express each answer as a signed rational and factor it: 1/k!, a binomial, a product of differences. Two agreeing cases suggest the form; confirm on a third. Treat any structural claim ("the only solution is...", "that coefficient vanishes") as a guess and test it on n = 2 before building on it. If a derivation stalls or contradicts itself, abandon it rather than restarting -- the checked small cases already fix the pattern. State the closed form with its sign and index shift.

Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, apply the stated markup multiplicatively, and check integrality and units.

Never open with a full set of unknown coefficients; that path always runs out of tokens. For an identity required to hold for all x, do not match coefficients. Instead guess a small structured family that satisfies it identically, then fit the given numbers. Ask what forces such maps to agree: a shared center c with each map of the form c plus or minus a*(x-c)^k, one map equal to the other plus a constant, or both iterates of a single map. Two unknowns plus the two given values is usually the whole problem. Also substitute the given special inputs into the identity for a free scalar equation, and check whether a requested input is itself the center, which makes its value immediate. When the problem asserts a unique answer, one family member meeting every stated condition suffices: verify it by direct substitution, then read off what is asked. A contradiction means the family is wrong, not the arithmetic; switch families instead of expanding further.

Treat each switcheroo as a permutation of positions. Label positions by fixed-width binary strings and determine which bit or block each stage changes; test the rule on the smallest sizes to fix indexing conventions. Compose the stages into one bitwise affine permutation. Determine its order from the cycle structure and prove minimality by exhibiting a position with the full cycle length.
